<reason>CON opened stronger by exposing PRO's ban-versus-neutrality strawman and forcing the debate onto what "same basic terms" means, but PRO adapted well and won that definitional clash. PRO's textual point—that "once safety standards are met" builds the pre-market gate into the motion itself—neutralized CON's central closing claim that a product needing permission is on different terms. PRO also directly answered CON's vacuity trap by naming concrete violations (name bans, warning labels, procurement exclusion), and turned CON's own "farm-raised"/"from concentrate" examples against it, prompting CON to retreat from "the label clash is over, CON won it" to "the label was never what made the regime different." CON's three bespoke elements were real but PRO's framework answer (different controls inside one regime, "a hazard is not a regime") plausibly covers them, and PRO showed CON's own preferred outcome—legal sale, inspection, truthful label, shelf access—is essentially the motion. Both sides had a clipped turn; both used grounded background knowledge without fake precision. Competitive, but PRO made the decision easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2 A1/A2: naming specific requirements that would violate the motion (defeating the "contentless" charge), then using CON's own salmon/juice disclosure examples to show origin qualifiers don't create a "different regime," forcing CON to abandon its earlier label victory.</best_rebuttal>
